title: Introduction to Backtracking
excerpt: Some problems have no formula and you simply have to search. Backtracking is how you search without doing an impossible amount of work, and it is one template you will reuse for the rest of the section.

content.text: Most of the algorithms you meet early on compute an answer. You feed them a graph or a list, they run a fixed procedure, and a result comes out. Backtracking is for the problems where no such procedure exists, and the only honest thing to do is try possibilities and see which ones survive.

Place eight queens on a chessboard so none attacks another. Fill in a Sudoku grid, or split a string so every piece reads the same forwards and backwards. There is no formula for any of these, and the only honest thing to do is try possibilities and see which ones survive.

The straightforward plan is to generate every possible arrangement and then throw away the ones that break the rules. It is simple, it is obviously correct, and for anything but toy inputs it does not finish.

Eight queens on a chessboard is a good illustration. Choosing 8 squares out of 64 gives a little over 4.4 billion arrangements to check. Almost all of them are absurd: they put two queens on the same square of the board's first row, or stack three in one column.

You can already improve on that by noticing something about the problem rather than about the code. Two queens in the same row always attack each other, so any valid solution has exactly one queen per row. Instead of choosing squares, choose a column for each of the 8 rows. That is 8 to the power of 8, which is about 16.7 million: still large, but nearly three hundred times smaller, and it came from thinking about the problem for a minute.

rows: Choose a column for each row
Choose a column, skipping ones already attacked

content.text: That last row is what this page is about, and the gap between it and the others is the whole reason backtracking is worth learning.

body.text: The idea: fail early, not at the end

content.text: Generate-and-filter has one specific weakness: it builds a complete arrangement before it checks anything. But you very often know an arrangement is doomed long before it is complete.

If the first two queens already attack each other, every single completion of that board is invalid. There are 8 to the power of 6 of them, which is 262,144 boards, and not one is worth building. Generate-and-filter builds all of them and rejects all of them individually.

So the idea is to build the answer one piece at a time, and to check the rules after each piece rather than at the end. The moment a partial answer is already broken, abandon it and everything that could have grown from it. Cutting off a whole family of possibilities with one check is called
pruning
, and it is where all the savings come from.

The word backtracking describes the other half. Having abandoned a partial answer, you have to get back to a state where you can try something else. You undo your last decision and try the next option. If there is no next option, you undo the decision before that. That walking-backwards-to-try-again is the backtrack.

body.text: Every one of these problems is secretly a tree

content.text: This is the mental model worth building carefully, because once you have it, every problem in this section looks like the same problem.

Think about the shape your search traces out. The root is the empty attempt, before you have decided anything. Each edge going down is one decision. Each node is the partial answer you have built so far. The leaves are complete attempts. Below is that tree, built live, for the smallest useful example: finding every subset of the numbers 1, 2 and 3, where each decision is simply whether to include the next number.

Notice that your own code never builds this tree as a data structure, even though the widget above is drawing exactly this shape for you as a teaching aid. The tree exists only as the shape your recursive calls trace out over time. Going down an edge is a function call, and returning from that call is the backtrack. It is a way of seeing what your program is doing, and once you can see it, pruning has an obvious meaning: it is cutting off an entire subtree, along with every leaf underneath it.

body.text: The template, which is genuinely always the same

content.text: Every problem in this section is this shape with different pieces filled in, and it is worth reading a few times, because the rest of the section is variations on it.
The three lines at the bottom are the heart of it, and they are always in that order. Choose, explore, un-choose. Miss the third and you carry a decision into branches where it was never made.
The
continue

above it is the prune. Everything you gain over brute force lives on that line, because skipping a choice there means the entire subtree below it is never built. In the queens table above, that single check is the difference between 16.7 million and 2,057.

body.text: A trace you can follow with a finger

content.text: Subsets is the gentlest place to watch the template run, because the rules never reject anything and you can concentrate on the shape of the recursion alone. Step through the same widget above again, and this time follow the call stack panel rather than the tree. Recursion depth is exactly how deep that stack goes, and every push is a choose, every pop is an undo.

Two things are worth noticing. Every recorded answer is a snapshot taken at that instant, and the underlying list being built is a single object being edited in place the entire run. It finishes empty, exactly as it started.

Also count the undos as you step through. There are exactly as many as there are chooses, and they always come back in the reverse order the choices were made. That symmetry is what keeps the state honest, and when a backtracking program misbehaves it is very often because that symmetry got broken somewhere.

Pruning is easier to believe than to picture, so here it is happening. This is the same template on a problem where the rules do reject candidates: combination sum, hunting for numbers from a fixed list that add up to a target. Flip pruning on and off and watch the two counters below the tree. Cutting overshooting branches early is the entire difference between them.
It is easy to underrate a single if statement, but the arithmetic is what makes the case.
In a tree where each node has
k
children and the tree runs
d
levels deep, cutting one node at depth
i
removes
k
to the power of
(d - i)
leaves. Cutting near the root is worth astronomically more than cutting near the bottom, which is why a cheap check applied early beats a clever check applied late.

The queens numbers make it concrete. Checking whether a square is attacked before placing a queen costs almost nothing and is done as early as possible, and it takes the search from 16.7 million completions down to 2,057 boards ever being built. The algorithm did not get smarter. It just stopped building things it already knew were worthless.

body.text: What it costs, and why exponential is not always fatal

content.text: There is no way around it: the worst case is exponential. Subsets of
n
items really does produce 2 to the power of
n
answers, and no algorithm can list them faster than it can print them. Permutations really do number
n
factorial. When the answer itself is exponentially large, the algorithm must be too.

What pruning changes is the gap between the worst case and the case in front of you. Those two are routinely separated by several orders of magnitude, and that gap is the difference between a program that returns and one that does not.

Memory is the reassuring part. At any moment you are holding one root-to-leaf path, so the space is proportional to the depth of the tree, not its size. A search that visits billions of nodes may only ever hold a few dozen items.

body.text: The bugs, in the order you will meet them

content.text: Forgetting to undo.
This is the classic, and its symptom is answers that get longer and longer as the run goes on, with items in them from branches you thought you had left.

The state is shared across every branch, so a choice made in one branch is still sitting there when a sibling branch runs. The fix is the missing line. The habit that prevents it is writing the undo immediately after writing the recursive call, before you do anything else.
Storing the working list instead of a copy of it is nearly as common a mistake and much more confusing, because the code looks right.

body.code:
answers.push(current);      // WRONG: stores a reference
answers.push([...current]); // right: stores a snapshot

content.text: The first line pushes a reference to the one list you keep editing. Since it finishes empty, every answer you collected turns out to be empty at the end, and the bug appears to come from nowhere. Take a snapshot at the moment you record.
Checking the rules only at the leaves.

Perfectly correct, and it quietly throws away every advantage backtracking has. If your solver is correct but far too slow, this is the first thing to look at: are you validating as early as you possibly could?
Pruning something that was actually valid.

The opposite failure, and the harder one to spot, because the program is fast and simply misses answers. When a solver returns 88 solutions to eight queens instead of 92, the prune is too aggressive rather than the search being broken.
Subsets written out. Compare it against the template above line by line and you will find every part of it, including the
start
parameter, which exists so that a choice already considered is not offered again further down.

variants.code:
def subsets(nums):
    answers = []
    current = []

    def solve(start):
        answers.append(current[:])     # a copy, see the note below

        for i in range(start, len(nums)):
            current.append(nums[i])    # choose
            solve(i + 1)               # explore
            current.pop()              # un-choose

    solve(0)
    return answers

content.text: From here the rest of the section changes only what goes in the blanks. Permutations swap the
start
parameter for a used-marker. N-Queens adds a real prune. Sudoku adds a rule about which blank to fill next. The skeleton does not move.

questions.prompt: What does pruning actually remove from the search?

options.label: The entire subtree below the pruned node, including every leaf under it
Duplicate answers found earlier in the run

questions.prompt: Your subsets solver returns the right number of answers, but they are all empty lists. What is wrong?

options.label: You stored the working list itself instead of a copy, and it ends empty
The start parameter is off by one

questions.prompt: Why is cutting a branch near the root worth far more than cutting one near the leaves?

options.label: The number of leaves removed grows exponentially with the remaining depth
Nodes near the root are more expensive to evaluate
It reduces the memory used by the recursion

questions.prompt: A backtracking search visits billions of nodes. Roughly how much memory does the recursion hold?

options.label: Proportional to the depth of the tree, since only one path is live at a time
Proportional to the number of nodes visited
Proportional to the number of answers found

questions.prompt: An N-Queens solver runs fast but reports 88 solutions instead of 92. What is the likeliest cause?

options.label: A prune is rejecting some placements that were actually legal
The recursion is hitting a depth limit

seoTitle: Introduction to Backtracking: The Algorithm Template Explained
seoDescription: Backtracking explained from first principles: why generate-and-filter dies, how pruning cuts whole subtrees, the choose-explore-unchoose template, a full hand trace, and the bugs everyone hits once.
